 Inspiration 

 Applying for jobs can be exhausting. You can spend hours searching through listings, comparing requirements, figuring out where your skills fit, and writing a different cover letter for every application. 

 AI agents can make a lot of that process much faster. They can search, analyze job descriptions, identify skill gaps, and even write application drafts. But there is one part we didn't want an agent to handle on its own: actually submitting the application . 

 That led us to the idea behind EzApply . 

 We wanted to build something where the agent takes care of the repetitive work, while the candidate stays in control of the decisions that matter. When we came across WebMCP , it felt like a natural fit. Instead of an agent trying to scrape a page or interact with a UI blindly, WebMCP lets the website expose structured tools that an agent can use directly. 

 So we thought: what if applying for jobs felt less like filling out endless forms and more like having an AI co-pilot? 

 That's what EzApply is built around. 

 What it does 

 EzApply is a Job Application Command Center built with WebMCP. 

 The agent can take a job from discovery all the way to a ready-to-submit application, but the candidate always has the final say. 

 We currently expose six WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_jobs — Finds jobs based on keywords, salary requirements, and remote preferences. 
 score_job_fit — Compares the candidate's skills with a job's requirements and calculates a fit percentage. 
 identify_skill_gap — Shows which skills are missing and gives suggestions for improving the candidate's resume. 
 generate_application_draft — Creates a tailored cover letter and sends it to the Approval Queue. 
 save_to_drafts — Saves changes made by the candidate to an AI-generated application. 
 submit_application — Handles the final submission, but only after the candidate explicitly confirms it. 
 

 Human-in-the-Loop Approval 

 This is the part of EzApply we're most proud of. 

 AI can prepare an application, but it doesn't get to decide when it is submitted. 

 Every generated application goes into an Approval Queue . The candidate can read the cover letter, make changes directly, and then approve it. 

 The submit_application tool also checks for candidateConfirmation: true inside its execute() function. This means the safety check isn't only part of the interface. The tool itself refuses to submit an application without explicit confirmation. 

 We wanted this to be a real safety boundary rather than just a button that looks like one. 

 Agent Console 

 We also wanted users to understand what the agent was actually doing. 

 The Agent Console displays WebMCP tool calls as they happen, including timestamps and status information. This makes the agent's actions visible instead of turning the whole process into a black box. 

 The 1-Click Pipeline 

 EzApply also has a one-click workflow that demonstrates how the tools can work together: 

 Search → Score → Identify Skill Gaps → Generate Draft → Human Review 

 The agent handles the tedious parts in sequence, while the candidate takes over when a decision actually matters. 

 How we built it 

 One of our goals was to keep the project simple enough that the WebMCP integration remained the focus. 

 The entire application is contained in a single HTML file of roughly 70KB , with inline CSS and JavaScript and no production dependencies. 

 We register our tools through document.modelContext using WebMCP's registerTool() API and provide proper inputSchema definitions so an agent knows what each tool expects. 

 For example: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_jobs" , 
 description : "Searches available tech jobs by keywords, salary, and remote status." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 query : { 
 type : "string" , 
 description : "Job title or skill keyword" 
 } , 
 minSalary : { 
 type : "number" 
 } , 
 remoteOnly : { 
 type : "boolean" 
 } 
 } , 
 required : [ "query" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const results = jobs . filter ( j = > matchesQuery ( j , input ) ) ; 

 return { 
 success : true , 
 count : results . length , 
 jobs : results
 } ; 
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 We also added a small in-memory modelContext fallback. If WebMCP isn't available in the browser, the app can still be explored normally. When WebMCP is available, the same tools are exposed through the native protocol. 

 For the interface, we went with an aviation-inspired command-center theme. Job cards look like boarding passes, jobs have flight-style codes, and the overall interface is designed to feel like you're managing a journey from discovery to application. 

 The project is deployed on Vercel using Vite as a minimal static setup. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the human approval step right 

 We didn't want the approval step to feel like unnecessary friction. At the same time, we didn't want to hide an important decision behind a single confirmation button. 

 We ended up using an inline-editable application draft so the candidate can make changes without leaving the workflow. The approval card is intentionally prominent, making it clear that this is the point where the human takes control. 

 Making WebMCP visible 

 One challenge with a protocol like WebMCP is that most of the interesting work happens behind the scenes. 

 A user doesn't necessarily know that an agent just called search_jobs or score_job_fit . 

 That's why we built the Agent Console. It turns those normally invisible interactions into something users can actually watch, which also helped us understand and debug the agent workflow while building the project. 

 Keeping everything in one file 

 We deliberately challenged ourselves to keep the application lightweight.
